_comment: Threats to a web app, by the part of it they concern, STRIDE category, and the conditions under which they apply. Each names the ASVS and AISVS requirements that answer it; nothing here says a threat is handled, which is for the evidence about those requirements to show. Ported on 25 September 2026 from v1's rule-based model (server/src/design/threat-model.ts) without its likelihood and impact, at the owner's decision, and without its template controls, which are v1's own code. v1's three threats per outside API are one set here. T-31 onward are new in sv, for what v1 did not model: MCP tools, retrieval, several services, WebSockets, and several tenants. Read by sv (agnostic/crates/sv-report/src/threats.rs); v1 is to read it too, later. See agnostic/docs/THREAT-MODELING.md. Each requirement carries a few words naming what the threat and the requirement share (`because`), which the citation guard holds against both texts, as for the crosswalk.

elements.name: Browsers and the app
elements.description: Every page, form, and request a browser sends to the app.

elements.name: The app itself
elements.description: The app's code, the packages it depends on, and its configuration.

elements.name: The app's stored data
elements.description: Wherever the app keeps what it saves: a database, files on disk, and their backups.

elements.name: The AI model
elements.description: The AI service the app sends prompts to, and what comes back.

elements.name: Uploaded files
elements.description: Files people upload, where they are kept, and how they are served again.

elements.name: Email
elements.description: The service the app sends email through.

elements.name: Payments
elements.description: The payment provider and its messages back to the app.

elements.name: Programs using the app's API
elements.description: Other programs that connect with an API key.

elements.name: Outside services
elements.description: The other services the app calls over the network.

elements.name: Scheduled jobs
elements.description: Work the app does on a timer, with nobody present.

elements.name: Tools the model can use (MCP)
elements.description: Tools reached over the Model Context Protocol, and the servers that provide them.

elements.name: The documents the model searches
elements.description: The documents, embeddings, or vector database the app searches to answer (retrieval-augmented generation).

elements.name: The app's own services
elements.description: The separate services the app is made of, and the calls between them.

elements.name: Live connections (WebSockets)
elements.description: Connections a browser keeps open for messages in both directions.

threats.description: Someone signs in as another person by guessing a password, reusing a leaked one, or stealing a session cookie.

requirements.because: guessing a short password
a leaked or common password
password guessing and credential stuffing attacks
guessing a session token
a session cookie a script can read

threats.description: A signed-in person opens administrator pages or other people's records by changing a web address.

requirements.because: administrator pages restricted by permissions
access rules enforced on the server, not in the page
records restricted to the person with permission
fields of records restricted by permission
records returned with fields a person should not see

threats.description: Someone denies having signed in or changed something, and there is no reliable record of it.

requirements.because: a logged record of signing in
a logged record of refused attempts
a record that cannot be modified

threats.description: Crafted input (injection, a request forged from another site, oversized or unexpected fields) changes data or behavior.

requirements.because: input validated against expected values
input validation on the server
unexpected fields accepted into records
injection into database queries
injection into an HTML response
injection of script the browser executes
a request forged from another site
crafted object fields that pollute the JavaScript prototype

threats.description: Traffic is read on the network, or pages, caches, and error messages reveal what they should not.

requirements.because: error messages that reveal sensitive details
pages kept in a cache
pages that reveal signed-in data left in the browser after the session
network traffic read where an outdated TLS protocol version is enabled
traffic sent without enforced HTTPS (HSTS)
cookies sent over the network without Secure

threats.description: Floods of requests, slow connections, or huge request bodies make the app unavailable.

requirements.because: excessive requests that cause denial of service
requests for resource-demanding work that make the app unavailable

threats.description: Text typed by a person, or hidden inside a record, tricks the model into ignoring its instructions (prompt injection).

requirements.because: prompt injection in inputs that steer the model
prompt injection attempts detected
user text that overrides the system instructions
hidden text smuggled in before normalization
hidden characters in the input
special tokens injected into the model context

threats.description: The model reveals other people's records, or its own instructions.

requirements.because: records the model can reach, behind access controls
access decisions made by the model itself
responses that reveal the model's own instructions (the system prompt)
responses with records the person may not see

threats.description: Runaway or abusive use of the model runs up the AI bill, spends tokens without limit, or exhausts the provider's quota.

requirements.because: budgets for token use and spend
token usage tracked per user
a switch to halt the model
the kill-switch that halts runaway use, logged
rate limits on the model

threats.description: The AI provider's API key leaks, in logs, in a prompt, or in generated text, and someone else uses it.

requirements.because: the key exposed in the model's context or prompt
the key leaks from source code, instead of being kept in a secrets store
the key leaks less when access to secret assets is least privilege
the key leaks in logs, where logging credentials is not allowed

threats.description: The model makes a change the person did not intend, or one they are not allowed to make.

requirements.because: a change the model makes without the person's approval
actions the model is allowed to make, enforced by policy

threats.description: The model is used to produce or spread harmful content.

requirements.because: harmful content in prompts, scored by a classifier
harmful content in responses, blocked by a classifier

threats.description: A harmful file, such as a script disguised as an image or an SVG with code in it, is uploaded and later opened by someone else.

requirements.because: a file whose contents do not match its extension or image type
an uploaded script executed on the server
file paths built from uploaded names
an uploaded file served back with its own filename
uploaded file names served without encoding

threats.description: Oversized or endless uploads fill the disk.

requirements.because: oversized files beyond what the app can process
limits on uploads per person, as documented

threats.description: Someone downloads another person's file by guessing its address.

requirements.because: another person's file reached by its address, where data-specific access should be restricted

threats.description: Someone adds hidden recipients or content to an email through a form field.

requirements.because: form input injected into email

threats.description: Password reset emails are abused to take over an account.

requirements.because: a password reset that takes over the account
a reset link whose random token can be guessed
password reset requests sent in excessive numbers

threats.description: Card numbers end up stored or logged by the app.

requirements.because: card numbers sent in the URL
card numbers in the logging of payment details

threats.description: A fake "payment succeeded" message marks an order as paid.

requirements.because: a message from the payment provider, authenticated before it is trusted

threats.description: A leaked API key is used by someone else.

threats.description: A program hammers the API with requests.

threats.description: Data sent to an outside service is exposed if that service is breached or the connection is intercepted.

threats.description: Log entries are altered or deleted to hide what happened.

threats.description: A scheduled job runs twice at once, or a long one takes the app's resources and makes it unavailable.

threats.description: Someone reaches the app's MCP server without a valid token, or with a token meant for another service.
